questions.prompt: What scorecard correction does Chapter 6 make first?
choices: Public ownership automatically requires soft standards
Public status does not excuse weak discipline
Broad portfolios are always stronger than focused ones

explanation.gentle: The chapter begins by rejecting the idea that public companies must be managed softly.
explanation.direct: Thorndike attacks public-company softness as an excuse, not as a fact of nature.
explanation.competitive: Being public is not permission to get lazy.

questions.prompt: Why is Ralston Purina's setting difficult in this chapter?
choices: Because the company had no real portfolio choices left
Because broad sprawl and diluted attention made softness easier to hide
Because the chapter stops caring about economics

explanation.gentle: The company had grown broad enough to hide weak uses of capital and attention.
explanation.direct: Sprawl made the scorecard blurrier and softer.
explanation.competitive: Too much breadth let weakness dress up as scale.

questions.prompt: What does the phrase public LBO mean in this chapter?
choices: The company actually leaves the public market
Management copies private-equity slang without changing behavior
A public company adopts owner-like discipline while staying public

explanation.gentle: The company stays public, but the internal standards get harder.
explanation.direct: The title names a discipline standard, not a change in listing status.
explanation.competitive: Ownership stays put; the excuses do not.

questions.prompt: Sadie sees two side projects draining the strongest line. What fits Chapter 6 best?
choices: Keep all projects so the portfolio still looks broad
Cut the weaker projects if doing so strengthens the core economics
Add another side project to spread risk further

explanation.gentle: The chapter says focus tightening matters when it improves the stronger business.
explanation.direct: Choice B matches Stiritz's logic: breadth loses when it weakens the core.
explanation.competitive: Protect the engine, not the decorations.

questions.prompt: Which belief does Chapter 6 challenge most directly?
choices: Cuts and harsh tone automatically prove discipline
Public ownership can justify soft standards
Both A and B

explanation.gentle: The chapter rejects both excuses: softness because of public status and fake rigor because of harshness.
explanation.direct: Thorndike pushes against public-company drift and against toughness theater.
explanation.competitive: Soft excuses and loud costumes both fail here.

questions.prompt: Andre's club entered too many competitions and weakened all of them. What is the chapter's best diagnosis?
choices: The club is confusing broad reach with strong focus
The club should add even more commitments
The club is wisely avoiding all hard tradeoffs

explanation.gentle: The group spread effort too thin and weakened the strongest work.
explanation.direct: This is Chapter 6 in miniature: sprawl is diluting the core.

questions.prompt: Why is operating rigor necessary in addition to portfolio moves?
choices: Because buying and selling units prove discipline automatically
Because the remaining business has to become less tolerant of weak capital use too
Because public companies should avoid accountability after divestitures

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the internal standards have to get tougher, not just the portfolio headlines.
explanation.direct: Owner discipline is real only when the operating scorecard tightens after the moves.
explanation.competitive: The announcement means nothing if the survivors stay soft.

questions.prompt: What limit keeps Chapter 6 from turning into private-equity worship?
choices: Severity matters only when it improves the economics and clarifies the scorecard
Any harsher culture must be creating value
The public market should be ignored entirely

explanation.gentle: The chapter stays strict by asking whether harder standards actually make the business better.
explanation.direct: Harshness earns respect only when the economics become clearer and stronger afterward.
explanation.competitive: A rough style without a sharper scorecard is just theater.

questions.prompt: What makes Stiritz's discipline rational in Thorndike's frame?
choices: It makes management sound more dangerous
It pushes capital and attention toward a stronger, clearer core
It guarantees every cut will be popular

explanation.gentle: The discipline matters because the remaining business is supposed to get stronger and clearer.
explanation.direct: Thorndike makes better economics, not harsher style, the evidence that counts.
explanation.competitive: The proof is a tougher core, not a scarier memo.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 6 prepare the move toward Dick Smith in Chapter 7?
choices: It shows owner-like discipline inside a public company before the next chapter moves into family-control constraints
It argues that ownership structure no longer matters at all
It proves broad portfolios are always irrational

explanation.gentle: Stiritz tightens public-company discipline before the next case shifts to owner logic under family control.
explanation.direct: Chapter 6 hardens the scorecard in public markets, then Chapter 7 changes the ownership constraint.
explanation.competitive: First public softness gets cut down, then family structure takes its turn.
